Ontological Argument
on-tuh-LAH-jih-kul AR-gyoo-ment
noun phrase (philosophical theology)
From Greek ontos (of being, genitive of on, being, present participle of einai, to be) + Late Latin argumentum (proof, evidence, from arguere, to make clear, prove). The argument is “ontological” because it proceeds from the concept of God’s being — from the very idea of a necessarily existent being — rather than from empirical observation of the world. The label was coined by Immanuel Kant (Critique of Pure Reason, 1781) to describe and critique what Anselm of Canterbury had proposed in his Proslogion (ca. 1078).

Biblical Definition

The ontological argument is the classic theistic argument that God’s existence can be inferred from the concept of God alone — specifically, from the idea of a being than which nothing greater can be conceived. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109) formulated it in his Proslogion: God is “that than which nothing greater can be conceived” (id quo majus cogitari nequit); if such a being existed only as an idea (in the mind but not in reality), then a greater being — one existing in reality — could be conceived; therefore the being that exists only in the mind is not truly the greatest, and God must exist in reality. The argument’s Reformed interest lies not primarily in its demonstrative validity (which most Reformed scholastics questioned) but in what it rightly signals: God is not a contingent being who might or might not exist depending on external conditions. He is self-existent — I AM WHO I AM (Exod. 3:14) — the one in whom essence and existence coincide, who cannot not exist. Hebrews 11:6 demands that the one approaching God “must believe that He is” — not as the conclusion of a syllogism but as the presupposition of all engagement with Him. The fool who says “there is no God” (Ps. 14:1) suppresses the sensus divinitatis and denies what he already knows; he does not reason to a different conclusion but willfully disbelieves what is evident.

Webster 1828 Definition

The classic philosophical argument, formulated by Anselm of Canterbury (Proslogion, ca. 1078), that God’s existence follows from the very concept of God as the greatest possible being; Reformed theology affirms what it rightly signals about divine aseity while remaining cautious about its demonstrative force as a standalone proof.

ONTOLOGICAL ARGUMENT, n. [Gk. ontos, of being] The theistic argument proposing that the concept of God as the greatest possible being necessarily implies His real existence — for a God existing only as an idea would be lesser than one existing in reality, contradicting the definition of God as the greatest.

2. Formulated by Anselm (Proslogion, ca. 1078); reformulated by Descartes (Meditations, 1641) and Leibniz; critiqued by Kant (1781) as illicitly deriving existence from a concept; revived in modal form by Alvin Plantinga (The Nature of Necessity, 1974): if God’s existence is possible and God is a necessary being, then God necessarily exists.

3. Reformed reception: the scholastics (Turretin, Owen, Bavinck) generally preferred the cosmological and teleological arguments as empirically grounded; the ontological argument’s power is conceptual — it exposes the assumption that existence is something God must earn from outside, whereas aseity means God’s being is the foundation of all being.

4. Kant’s critique: existence is not a predicate — one cannot derive “exists” from a concept alone. Reformed rejoinder: for God uniquely, existence IS essential; He is the I AM (Exod. 3:14), the self-existent One for whom existence is not a contingent addition to an essence but the very heart of who He is.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 11:6 — "And without faith it is impossible to please Him — for he who comes to God must believe that He is, and that He is a rewarder of those who seek Him."

Exodus 3:14 — "And God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM.” And He said, “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel, ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”"

Psalm 14:1 — "The fool has said in his heart, “There is no God.” They are corrupt, They have done abominable works, There is none who does good."

Romans 1:20 — "For since the creation of the world His invisible attributes — His eternal power and divine nature — have been clearly seen, being understood through what has been made. So they are without excuse."

Modern Corruption

Modern atheism treats God’s existence as a hypothesis awaiting external empirical proof, inverting the biblical reality that God’s self-existence is the precondition of all thought and being; the ontological argument, whatever its logical weaknesses, rightly diagnoses this inversion.

expand to see more

The New Atheism (Dawkins, Hitchens, Harris, Dennett) frames God’s existence as an empirical hypothesis about the physical universe — one that science can in principle test and falsify. This presupposes that God, if He exists, is one item among the universe’s contents, subject to empirical investigation like any natural phenomenon. The ontological argument, for all its metaphysical abstraction, at least grasped the opposite: God is not a contingent being in need of external cause but the self-existent One in whom “we live, and move, and exist” (Acts 17:28). To demand empirical proof of God’s existence is to assume He is an item inside the universe He created — a category error the Proslogion and the Reformed doctrine of aseity both expose.

Process theologians (Whitehead, Griffin, Cobb) revised the concept of God to make Him finite, growing, and dependent on the world — a God who needs the universe and is in some sense shaped by it. This is the inverse of the ontological argument’s core insight: a God who depends on anything outside Himself for any aspect of His being is not the God of Scripture (Job 38–41; Isa. 40:12–31). The Reformed doctrine of divine aseity — that God has life in Himself (John 5:26), depends on nothing, and is the source of all being — is not philosophical speculation but the scriptural portrait of the living God. The ontological argument’s attempt to reason from the concept of a necessary being captures a genuine truth even when its logical form fails: God’s existence is not contingent, not dependent, and not something He borrows from the world.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Greek ontos (of being) + argumentum (proof); the argument reasons from being itself — from the concept of a self-existent Creator — and rightly signals that God’s existence is necessary rather than contingent, even if the argument’s logical form has been contested from Kant onward.

expand to see more

Greek on / ontos — being, that-which-is; ontology is the study of being as such; the argument is “ontological” because it reasons about God from the category of necessary existence rather than from observed contingent effects in the world

Latin aseitas — self-existence, from a se (from oneself); the Reformed doctrine of aseity captures what the ontological argument rightly pointed toward: God’s being is underived, self-sufficient, and prior to all else

Hebrew ’ehyeh — I AM, I will be (Exod. 3:14); God’s self-identification as I AM WHO I AM is the biblical ground for what philosophers call necessary existence — His name is His nature, and His nature is simply to be

Latin necessarium — necessary, not-able-not-to-be; what philosophers call “necessary existence” Scripture names with the divine name — God cannot not exist, for He is the foundation of existence itself, not one instance of it

Greek mōros — fool; the Psalm 14 “fool” who denies God does not reason to a logical conclusion but suppresses what is already known — atheism is not a philosophical position but a moral posture of suppression

Usage

"The ontological argument is best used not as a knockdown proof but as a conceptual corrective: it exposes the secular assumption that God must prove His existence from within a system that already presupposes His absence — a presupposition that itself requires justification."

"Alvin Plantinga’s modal version of the ontological argument — arguing that if God’s existence is possible and God is a necessary being, then God necessarily exists — has earned serious engagement from analytic philosophers, including many who do not share his Reformed faith, and has made theism once again philosophically respectable in the academy."

"The Reformed tradition’s primary confidence in God’s existence rests not on any philosophical argument but on the sensus divinitatis — the innate God-knowledge Calvin found in Romans 1 — combined with the Spirit’s testimony applied to the gospel of Christ; arguments serve the church but do not establish the faith."
